claim: The heat shock response is a universal homeostatic cell autonomous reaction of organisms to cope with adverse environmental conditions.
source: The heat shock response is a universal homeostatic cell autonomous reaction of organisms to cope with adverse environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a general statement about the heat shock response that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In mammalian cells, the heat shock response is mediated by the heat shock transcription factor Hsf1.
source: In mammalian cells, this response is mediated by the heat shock transcription factor Hsf1, which is monomeric in unstressed cells and upon activation trimerizes, and binds to promoters of heat shock genes.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and is consistent with the experimental design of the study.

claim: Hsf1 is monomeric in unstressed cells.
source: In mammalian cells, this response is mediated by the heat shock transcription factor Hsf1, which is monomeric in unstressed cells and upon activation trimerizes, and binds to promoters of heat shock genes.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1B and 1C, as well as established knowledge.

claim: Upon activation, Hsf1 trimerizes and binds to promoters of heat shock genes.
source: In mammalian cells, this response is mediated by the heat shock transcription factor Hsf1, which is monomeric in unstressed cells and upon activation trimerizes, and binds to promoters of heat shock genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 1C and 1D showing trimerization and DNA binding after heat shock.

claim: Temperature-induced alterations in the conformational dynamics of Hsf1 were analyzed by hydrogen exchange mass spectrometry.
source: To understand the basic principle of Hsf1 activation we analyzed temperature-induced alterations in the conformational dynamics of Hsf1 by hydrogen exchange mass spectrometry.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: Temperature-dependent unfolding of Hsf1 occurs in the regulatory region concomitant to tighter packing in the trimerization region.
source: We found a temperature-dependent unfolding of Hsf1 in the regulatory region happening concomitant to tighter packing in the trimerization region.
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS data shown in Figure 2, demonstrating increased exchange in HR-C and decreased exchange in HR-A/B with temperature.

claim: The transition to the active DNA binding-competent state occurred highly cooperative and was concentration dependent.
source: The transition to the active DNA binding-competent state occurred highly cooperative and was concentration dependent.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 2, 6, and 7 showing steep transition curves and concentration-dependent activation.

claim: Hsp90 lowered the midpoint temperature of trimerization and reduced cooperativity of the process thus widening the response window.
source: Surprisingly, Hsp90, known to inhibit Hsf1 activation, lowered the midpoint temperature of trimerization and reduced cooperativity of the process thus widening the response window.
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS and EMSA data shown in Figure 8.

claim: In all eukaryotic cells, heat shock transcription factor (HSF) 1 is the master regulator of the heat shock response.
source: In all eukaryotic cells, heat shock transcription factor (HSF) 1 is the master regulator of this response and alters transcription of a large number of genes, some of which encode chaperones and proteases (Anckar and Sistonen, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Hsf1 alters transcription of a large number of genes, some of which encode chaperones and proteases.
source: In all eukaryotic cells, heat shock transcription factor (HSF) 1 is the master regulator of this response and alters transcription of a large number of genes, some of which encode chaperones and proteases (Anckar and Sistonen, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Systemic modulation of the heat shock response has been observed in metazoa.
source: Although this response is essentially cell autonomous, systemic modulation of this response has been observed in metazoa (Morimoto, 2008; Prahlad et al., 2008; Prahlad and Morimoto, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Metazoan Hsf1 consists of a N-terminal winged helix-turn-helix DNA binding domain.
source: Metazoan Hsf1 consists of a N-terminal winged helix-turn-helix DNA binding domain (Harrison et al., 1994; Vuister et al., 1994), a hydrophobic shorter heptad repeat regions (HR-A/B) proposed to function as a leucine zipper coiled-coil trimerization domain (Clos et al., 1990; Rabindran et al., 1993), a regulatory domain, a second heptad repeat (HR-C) and a C-terminal transcription activation domain (Figure 1A) (Anckar and Sistonen, 2011; Voellmy, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and is shown in Figure 1A.

claim: HR-A/B is proposed to function as a leucine zipper coiled-coil trimerization domain.
source: Metazoan Hsf1 consists of a N-terminal winged helix-turn-helix DNA binding domain (Harrison et al., 1994; Vuister et al., 1994), a hydrophobic shorter heptad repeat regions (HR-A/B) proposed to function as a leucine zipper coiled-coil trimerization domain (Clos et al., 1990; Rabindran et al., 1993), a regulatory domain, a second heptad repeat (HR-C) and a C-terminal transcription activation domain (Figure 1A) (Anckar and Sistonen, 2011; Voellmy, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In unstressed cells metazoan Hsf1 is monomeric and supposed to be in complex with molecular chaperones, including Hsp70, Hsp90 and TRiC/CCT.
source: In unstressed cells metazoan Hsf1 is monomeric and supposed to be in complex with molecular chaperones, including Hsp70, Hsp90 and TRiC/CCT (Shi et al., 1998; Zou et al., 1998; Neef et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: At physiological concentrations monomeric Hsf1 does not bind appreciably to heat shock elements (nGAAn).
source: At physiological concentrations monomeric Hsf1 does not bind appreciably to heat shock elements (nGAAn).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data in Figure 1D and established knowledge.

claim: In the activated state Hsf1 forms trimers or higher order oligomers and binds to its response elements in heat shock gene promoters.
source: In the activated state Hsf1 forms trimers or higher order oligomers and binds to its response elements in heat shock gene promoters (Clos et al., 1990; Rabindran et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations and experimental data in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: Deletion or mutational alteration of HR-C leads to constitutive trimerization.
source: Based on the observation that deletion or mutational alteration of HR-C leads to constitutive trimerization Wu and co-workers proposed that Hsf1 is a thermosensor itself and kept monomeric by intramolecular leucine zipper formation (Rabindran et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Activation of human Hsf1 in human and insect cells and Xenopus oocytes occurs at different temperatures.
source: However, activation of human Hsf1 in human and insect cells and Xenopus oocytes occurs at different temperatures, arguing against an Hsf1 intrinsic mechanism of heat shock activation (Baler et al., 1993; Clos et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chaperones were proposed to prevent Hsf1 activation and to be titrated away from Hsf1 under stress conditions.
source: Owing to the fact that the large variety of Hsf1-inducing signals have in common to cause protein misfolding and in analogy to the regulation of the heat shock response in E. coli (Guisbert et al., 2008), chaperones were proposed to prevent Hsf1 activation and to be titrated away from Hsf1 under stress conditions, resulting in heat shock response induction (Morimoto, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Inhibition of Hsp70, Hsp90 or TRiC/CCT or knock-down of their expression leads to the induction of the heat shock response.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis is the observation that inhibition of Hsp70, Hsp90 or TRiC/CCT or knock-down of their expression leads to the induction of the heat shock response (Powers and Workman, 2007; Powers et al., 2008; Neef et al., 2014; Whitesell et al., 2003; Lee et al., 2013; Abravaya et al., 1992; Zou et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Recombinant human Hsf1 was purified out of E. coli by affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography, resulting in mostly monomeric species in the final fraction.
source: Recombinant human Hsf1 was purified out of E. coli by affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography, resulting in mostly monomeric species in the final fraction (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by the chromatography data shown in Figure 1B and blue native gel in Figure 1C.

claim: Upon incubation at 42°C, Hsf1 formed trimers and higher-order oligomers.
source: Upon incubation at 42°C, Hsf1 formed trimers and higher-order oligomers, as verified by blue native gel electrophoresis consistent with published data (Clos et al., 1990), and acquired DNA-binding competence as shown by electrophoretic mobility shift assays (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by blue native gel data in Figure 1C and EMSA data in Figure 1D, as well as citation to previous work.

claim: Hsf1 acquired DNA-binding competence upon heat shock at 42°C.
source: Upon incubation at 42°C, Hsf1 formed trimers and higher-order oligomers, as verified by blue native gel electrophoresis consistent with published data (Clos et al., 1990), and acquired DNA-binding competence as shown by electrophoretic mobility shift assays (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Monomeric Hsf1 is highly dynamic with only few regions exhibiting significant protection from hydrogen exchange.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, monomeric Hsf1 is highly dynamic with only few regions exhibiting significant protection from HX, including parts of the DNA binding domain and the trimerization domain (HR-A/B).
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Parts of the DNA binding domain and the trimerization domain (HR-A/B) exhibit significant protection from hydrogen exchange in monomeric Hsf1.
source: As shown in Figure 1E, monomeric Hsf1 is highly dynamic with only few regions exhibiting significant protection from HX, including parts of the DNA binding domain and the trimerization domain (HR-A/B).
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Out of the C-terminal half of Hsf1, only the HR-C region showed significant protection at 20°C.
source: Out of the C-terminal half of the protein, containing the regulatory region, HR-C and the transactivation domain, only the HR-C region showed significant protection at 20°C consistent with an earlier study showing the C-terminal half of Hsf1 largely unfolded (Pattaramanon et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS data in Figure 1E and citation to previous work.

claim: The 10 min-pre-incubation of Hsf1 dramatically changed conformational dynamics of two regions in Hsf1: temperature-dependent increase in HX is observed in HR-C, and a concomitant decrease in HX is observed in HR-A/B.
source: The 10 min-pre-incubation of Hsf1 dramatically changed conformational dynamics of two regions in Hsf1 (Figure 2): temperature-dependent increase in HX is observed in HR-C, indicating heat-induced unfolding, and a concomitant decrease in HX is observed in HR-A/B, consistent with heat-induced trimerization.
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS data shown in Figure 2C-G.

claim: Temperature-dependent increase in HX in HR-C indicates heat-induced unfolding.
source: The 10 min-pre-incubation of Hsf1 dramatically changed conformational dynamics of two regions in Hsf1 (Figure 2): temperature-dependent increase in HX is observed in HR-C, indicating heat-induced unfolding, and a concomitant decrease in HX is observed in HR-A/B, consistent with heat-induced trimerization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HX-MS data shown in Figure 2, where increased exchange indicates unfolding.

claim: Concomitant decrease in HX in HR-A/B is consistent with heat-induced trimerization.
source: The 10 min-pre-incubation of Hsf1 dramatically changed conformational dynamics of two regions in Hsf1 (Figure 2): temperature-dependent increase in HX is observed in HR-C, indicating heat-induced unfolding, and a concomitant decrease in HX is observed in HR-A/B, consistent with heat-induced trimerization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HX-MS data shown in Figure 2, where decreased exchange indicates stabilization through trimerization.

claim: Bimodal distributions of the isotope clusters are indicative of the coexistence of two populations of molecules with different exchange properties.
source: Close inspection of the spectra of the peptic fragments exhibiting temperature-induced changes in HX revealed bimodal distributions of the isotope clusters indicative of the coexistence of two populations of molecules with different exchange properties (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mass spectrometry data shown in the figures.

claim: For the HR-A/B region the relative frequency of high exchanging population decreases with pre-incubation at increasing temperatures resulting in a sigmoidal temperature response curve.
source: For the HR-A/B region the relative frequency of high exchanging population decreases with pre-incubation at increasing temperatures resulting in a sigmoidal temperature response curve (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For the HR-C region the frequency of high exchanging species increased with increasing temperatures.
source: For the HR-C region the opposite is observed: the frequency of high exchanging species increased with increasing temperatures (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Hsf1 has intrinsic thermosensory properties.
source: These data clearly demonstrate that Hsf1 has intrinsic thermosensory properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HX-MS data showing temperature-dependent conformational changes in isolated Hsf1.

claim: The midpoint of transition Tm after 10 min was identical for both HR-A/B and HR-C regions equal to 36.15 ± 0.14°C.
source: The midpoint of transition Tm, the temperature at which 50% of the molecules are in the high exchanging conformation after 10 min, was identical for both regions equal to 36.15 ± 0.14°C.
evidence: This is derived from fitting the thermal unfolding equation to the data in Figures 2E and 2G.

claim: At 30 min pre-incubation, the transition curves became more shallow, and the midpoint temperature for HR-C unfolding and HR-A protection (trimerization) was not identical anymore but decreased to 32.0 ± 0.4 and 34.7 ± 0.2°C, respectively.
source: Under these prolonged incubation conditions, the transition curves became more shallow, and the midpoint temperature for HR-C unfolding and HR-A protection (trimerization) was not identical anymore but decreased to 32.0 ± 0.4 and 34.7 ± 0.2°C, respectively.
evidence: This is derived from fitting the data shown in Figure 2E and 2G for 30-min incubation.

claim: The temperature-induced conformational changes are not reversible under the experimental conditions.
source: These data suggest that the temperature-induced conformational changes are not reversible under our conditions, otherwise the steepness of the curves, which is determined by the unfolding enthalpy, should remain the same as for the 10-min-pre-incubation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that longer incubation times result in shallower curves and lower Tm values.

claim: HR-C unfolding, HR-A protection and Hsf1 trimerization are not reversible under the experimental conditions.
source: Both assays clearly demonstrate that HR-C unfolding, HR-A protection and Hsf1 trimerization are not reversible under these conditions.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3 showing that prolonged incubation at 20°C after heat shock does not revert the conformational changes.

claim: For the peptic fragments of HR-C the low-exchanging population decrease with rates of 0.0028 ± 0.0002, 0.0038 ± 0.0002, 0.011 ± 0.001, and 0.018 ± 0.001 s-1 at 35, 37, 39 and 42°C, respectively.
source: For the peptic fragments of HR-C (amino acids 378–395 and 389–395) the low-exchanging population decrease with a rate of 0.0028 ± 0.0002, 0.0038 ± 0.0002, 0.011 ± 0.001, and 0.018 ± 0.001 s-1 at 35, 37, 39 and 42°C, respectively.
evidence: This is derived from fitting exponential equations to the kinetic data shown in Figure 4.

claim: For the peptic fragments of HR-A/B the low-exchanging population increased with rates of 0.0018 ± 0.0004, 0.0033 ± 0.0002, 0.0094 ± 0.0009 and 0.016 ± 0.001 s-1 at 35, 37, 39 and 42°C, respectively.
source: For the peptic fragments of HR-A/B (amino acids 159–168 and 169–175) the low-exchanging population increased with slightly lower rates of 0.0018 ± 0.0004, 0.0033 ± 0.0002, 0.0094 ± 0.0009 and 0.016 ± 0.001 s-1 (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is derived from fitting exponential equations to the kinetic data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Arrhenius plot of the kinetic data yielded the activation energy for the temperature transition of 249 ± 47 kJ·mol-1.
source: The Arrhenius plot of the data yielded the activation energy for the temperature transition of 249 ± 47 kJ·mol-1 (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is derived from the Arrhenius plot shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Hsf1 is a thermosensor that directly senses increasing temperatures with conformational changes in HR-A/B and HR-C.
source: Taken together, our data demonstrate that Hsf1 is a thermosensor that directly senses increasing temperatures with conformational changes in HR-A/B and HR-C.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HX-MS data showing temperature-dependent conformational changes.

claim: Replacement of hydrophobic heptad repeat residues in HR-A by serine results in constitutively unfolded HR-A/B and HR-C at all temperatures tested.
source: HX-MS experiments with the mutant protein revealed that HR-A/B and HR-C are constitutively unfolded at all temperatures tested (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ability of HR-A to form a coiled-coil is essential for stabilization of HR-A, HR-B and HR-C.
source: These results demonstrate that the ability of HR-A to form a coiled-coil is essential for stabilization of HR-A, HR-B and HR-C, suggesting that HR-C also interacts with HR-A.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutations preventing coiled-coil formation lead to unfolding of both HR-A/B and HR-C.

claim: HR-C interacts with HR-A.
source: These results demonstrate that the ability of HR-A to form a coiled-coil is essential for stabilization of HR-A, HR-B and HR-C, suggesting that HR-C also interacts with HR-A.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutant data showing that HR-C stability depends on HR-A coiled-coil formation.

claim: The midpoint of trimerization of Hsf1 in vitro was around 36°C.
source: In our in vitro experiments, the midpoint of trimerization of Hsf1 was around 36°C, which seemed rather low given a body core temperature of 37°C, and DNA binding activity of Hsf1 in different human cells is rather low below 40°C and strongly increased above 42°C (Abravaya et al., 1991; Mosser et al., 1990; Baler et al., 1993).
evidence: This is derived from the HX-MS data and compared to literature values for cellular activation.

claim: DNA binding activity of Hsf1 in different human cells is rather low below 40°C and strongly increased above 42°C.
source: In our in vitro experiments, the midpoint of trimerization of Hsf1 was around 36°C, which seemed rather low given a body core temperature of 37°C, and DNA binding activity of Hsf1 in different human cells is rather low below 40°C and strongly increased above 42°C (Abravaya et al., 1991; Mosser et al., 1990; Baler et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In testis the major increase in DNA binding activity of Hsf1 is already observed at 38°C.
source: In contrast, in testis the major increase in DNA binding activity of Hsf1 is already observed at 38°C (Sarge, 1995; Sarge et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Trimerization as multi-molecular reaction would be intrinsically concentration dependent.
source: Trimerization as multi-molecular reaction would be intrinsically concentration dependent.
evidence: This is based on fundamental principles of chemical equilibria.

claim: Inhibition of trimerization by coiled-coil interaction of HR-C with HR-A/B would be an intramolecular reaction and consequently independent of concentration.
source: In contrast, inhibition of trimerization by coiled-coil interaction of HR-C with HR-A/B, as originally proposed by Wu and colleagues (Rabindran et al., 1993), would be an intramolecular reaction and consequently independent of concentration.
evidence: This is based on fundamental principles of chemical equilibria and cites the original model.

claim: Spontaneous trimerization of Hsf1 occurs even at 4°C upon concentrating the protein.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis we noticed spontaneous trimerization of Hsf1 even at 4°C upon concentrating the protein.
evidence: This is an observation made during the experimental work.

claim: For 100 nM Hsf1, no activation was observed up to 42°C.
source: For 100 nM Hsf1, no activation was observed up to 42°C (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: At 300 nM Hsf1, less than 20% of the theoretical possible Hsf1 trimers had formed at 42°C within 10 min.
source: At 300 nM, less than 20% of the theoretical possible Hsf1 trimers had formed at 42°C within 10 min.
evidence: This is derived from the fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: At 1 and 5 µM concentrations a substantial fraction of Hsf1 trimers had formed already at lower temperatures.
source: In contrast, at 1 and 5 µM concentrations a substantial fraction of Hsf1 trimers had formed already at lower temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence anisotropy data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The difference in transition temperature between Hsf1 at 5 µM and at 2 µM was highly statistically significant (p<0.0001).
source: However, the difference in transition temperature between Hsf1 at 5 µM and at 2 µM was highly statistically significant (p<0.0001).
evidence: This is derived from statistical analysis of the HX-MS data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: HR-C unfolding, trimerization and the fraction of DNA-competent Hsf1 trimers are a function of temperature and concentration.
source: Taken together, these data clearly demonstrate that HR-C unfolding, trimerization and the fraction of DNA-competent Hsf1 trimers are a function of temperature and concentration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined HX-MS and fluorescence anisotropy data.

claim: Human Hsf1 is heavily modified by posttranslational modifications (29 phosphorylation sites, 5 acetylation sites and 1 sumoylation site).
source: Human Hsf1 is heavily modified by posttranslational modifications (29 phosphorylation sites, 5 acetylation sites and 1 sumoylation site; www.phosphosite.org).
evidence: This is based on information from a database of posttranslational modifications.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser307 was proposed to negatively regulate the activation of Hsf1.
source: Phosphorylation of Ser307 was proposed to negatively regulate the activation of Hsf1, because Hsf1-S307A was constitutively active in vivo (Chu et al., 1996; Xia et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser303 had no influence on Hsf1 activation.
source: In contrast, phosphorylation of the close-by Ser303 had no influence on Hsf1 activation (Xia et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The transition temperature for the phosphomimetic variants S303D and S307D was slightly but statistically significantly lower than for Hsf1wt.
source: The transition temperature for the phosphomimetic variants was slightly but statistically significantly lower than for Hsf1wt, indicating that phosphorylation at these sites does not prevent temperature-induced trimerization and might even aid it at physiological concentrations of Hsf1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Phosphorylation at Ser303 and Ser307 does not prevent temperature-induced trimerization and might even aid it at physiological concentrations of Hsf1.
source: The transition temperature for the phosphomimetic variants was slightly but statistically significantly lower than for Hsf1wt, indicating that phosphorylation at these sites does not prevent temperature-induced trimerization and might even aid it at physiological concentrations of Hsf1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that phosphomimetic variants have lower Tm values.

claim: In the presence of Hsp90 the midpoint of transition was lower than in its absence and the response curve was less steep.
source: Surprisingly, in the presence of Hsp90 the midpoint of transition was lower than in its absence and the response curve was less steep, stretching the transition window from ~10° in the absence of Hsp90 to ~20°.
evidence: This is supported by HX-MS and EMSA data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Hsp90 stretches the transition window from ~10° in its absence to ~20°.
source: Surprisingly, in the presence of Hsp90 the midpoint of transition was lower than in its absence and the response curve was less steep, stretching the transition window from ~10° in the absence of Hsp90 to ~20°.
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the temperature response curves in Figure 8.

claim: The midpoint temperature of transition in the presence of Hsp90 was slightly lower for the peptide derived from HR-C than for the HR-A/B peptides.
source: Interestingly, the midpoint temperature of transition in the presence of Hsp90 was slightly lower for the peptide derived from HR-C than for the HR-A/B peptides (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: The results of the DNA binding assay were identical to those of the HX-MS experiments within experimental error.
source: Within the experimental error, the results of the DNA binding assay were identical to those of the HX-MS experiments (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figure 8B, C, and F with Figure 8G.

claim: In an in vitro assay with purified components, Hsp90 neither inhibits Hsf1 trimerization nor its DNA binding but lowers transition temperature and widens the activation window.
source: Taken together, our results demonstrate that in an in vitro assay with purified components, Hsp90 neither inhibits Hsf1 trimerization nor its DNA binding but, on the contrary, lowers transition temperature and widens the activation window.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the HX-MS and EMSA data with Hsp90 shown in Figure 8.

claim: Human Hsf1 is a thermosensor.
source: In this study we demonstrate that human Hsf1 is a thermosensor.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental data.

claim: The HR-C region of Hsf1 unfolds with temperature-dependent rates, resulting in a release of its repressive effect on Hsf1 trimerization and DNA binding.
source: We are the first to show that the HR-C region of Hsf1 unfolds with temperature-dependent rates, resulting in a release of its repressive effect on Hsf1 trimerization and DNA binding.
evidence: This is supported by the HX-MS data showing temperature-dependent unfolding of HR-C and its correlation with trimerization.

claim: For relatively short heat shocks unfolding of HR-C and trimerization through intermolecular interactions of HR-A/B exhibit the same temperature response curves and follow identical kinetics.
source: For relatively short heat shocks unfolding of HR-C and trimerization through intermolecular interactions of HR-A/B exhibit the same temperature response curves and follow identical kinetics, suggesting that these are coupled events.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figures 2 and 4 showing identical Tm values and kinetics for 10-min incubations.

claim: HR-C unfolding and HR-A/B trimerization are coupled events for short heat shocks.
source: For relatively short heat shocks unfolding of HR-C and trimerization through intermolecular interactions of HR-A/B exhibit the same temperature response curves and follow identical kinetics, suggesting that these are coupled events.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of identical kinetics and Tm values.

claim: For longer heat shocks the cooperativity of the transition is reduced and HR-C unfolding and HR-A/B trimerization seem to uncouple.
source: For longer heat shocks the cooperativity of the transition is reduced and HR-C unfolding and HR-A/B trimerization seem to uncouple.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing different Tm values for HR-C and HR-A/B at 30-min incubation times.

claim: HR-C unfolding, temperature-induced trimerization and acquisition of DNA-binding competence depends on the concentration of Hsf1.
source: Most importantly, HR-C unfolding, temperature-induced trimerization and acquisition of DNA-binding competence depends on the concentration of Hsf1.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figures 6 and 7 showing concentration-dependent effects.

claim: Hsp90 significantly modulated the temperature response of Hsf1, reducing midpoint and steepness of the response curve.
source: Moreover, Hsp90 significantly modulated the temperature response of Hsf1, reducing midpoint and steepness of the response curve, thus widening the temperature window within which Hsf1 transits from monomer to trimer and low to maximal DNA binding competence.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 8.

claim: The response curves of Hsf1 in the presence of Hsp90 are similar to the response curves at prolonged incubation time at elevated temperatures.
source: The response curves of Hsf1 in the presence of Hsp90 are similar to the response curves at prolonged incubation time at elevated temperatures.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the curves in Figures 2 and 8.

claim: Hsp90 accelerates the response at intermediate heat shock conditions.
source: Thus, Hsp90 accelerates the response at intermediate heat shock conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Hsp90 produces similar effects to longer incubation times.

claim: Human HSF1 does not exist in a trimer-monomer equilibrium.
source: However, human HSF1 does not seem to exist in such an equilibrium, as we did not observe dissociation of trimeric human Hsf1 upon dilution and heat-induced trimerization was irreversible in our hands (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 3 showing no reversal of trimerization.

claim: There are principle differences between Drosophila and human Hsf1.
source: These data suggest that there are principle differences between Drosophila and human Hsf1.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences in reversibility of trimerization between Drosophila and human Hsf1.

claim: At low temperatures even rare unfolding fluctuations of HR-C will eventually lead to trimerization.
source: Therefore, at low temperatures even rare unfolding fluctuations of HR-C will eventually lead to trimerization, which will not be observed at short incubation times.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the differences between 10-min and 30-min incubation data.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser307 does not inhibit heat-induced trimerization but might rather favor it.
source: The temperature response curve of the phosphomimetic Hsf1-S307D variant measured by HX-MS showed a slightly reduced midpoint of transition as compared to wild-type Hsf1, suggesting that phosphorylation at this site does not inhibit heat-induced trimerization but might rather favor it and the repressive effect must be at a different level.
evidence: This is inferred from the HX-MS data showing lower Tm for the phosphomimetic variant.

claim: Hsp90 also inhibits the heat shock response in yeast, although yeast Hsf1 is constitutively trimeric and bound to DNA.
source: First, Hsp90 also inhibits the heat shock response in yeast, although yeast Hsf1 is constitutively trimeric and bound to DNA, suggesting that Hsp90 could exert its inhibiting function on human Hsf1 after trimerization and DNA binding as well, consistent with observations for human Hsf1 (Duina et al., 1998; Sorger et al., 1987; Guo et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on yeast and human Hsf1.

claim: Interaction of Hsp90 with Hsf1 seems only to be observed after cross-linking, suggesting a very transient interaction.
source: Third, effects of Hsp90 down-regulation or inhibition could also be indirect, especially because interaction of Hsp90 with Hsf1 seems only to be observed after cross-linking (Neef et al., 2014; Zou et al., 1998), suggesting a very transient interaction.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hsp90 chaperones many kinases, and inhibition of Hsp90 leads to inactivation and degradation of these client proteins.
source: Hsp90 chaperones many kinases, and inhibition of Hsp90 leads to inactivation and degradation of these client proteins.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Hsp90 function.

claim: Loss of kinases could reduce inhibitory effects of phosphorylation or phosphorylation-dependent sumoylation of Hsf1.
source: Loss of such kinases could reduce inhibitory effects of phosphorylation or phosphorylation-dependent sumoylation of Hsf1 (Soncin et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2006; Hietakangas et al., 2003; 2006).
evidence: This is a speculation about indirect effects of Hsp90 inhibition, supported by citations.

claim: HR-C forms a coiled-coil with HR-A or HR-B to prevent trimerization in unstressed HSF1.
source: Originally, it was proposed that HR-C forms a coiled-coil with HR-A or HR-B to prevent trimerization in unstressed HSF1 (Rabindran et al., 1993; Zuo et al., 1994).
evidence: This is a previously proposed model cited from the literature.

claim: Hsf1 spontaneously trimerizes at high concentrations in the absence of a heat shock.
source: Together with the observation that Hsf1 spontaneously trimerizes at high concentrations in the absence of a heat shock ([Zhong et al., 1998] and our own observations) and with our HX-MS data, showing temperature-induced unfolding of HR-C, the model shown in Figure 9A can be derived.
evidence: This is supported by citation and the authors' own observations.

claim: Under non-stress conditions, HSF1 is in a conformational equilibrium between a closed conformation with HR-C interacting with HR-A/B and an open conformation.
source: Under non-stress conditions, HSF1 is in a conformational equilibrium between a closed conformation with HR-C interacting with HR-A/B and an open conformation, in which the two heptad repeat regions are dissociated.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: The net charge of HR-A/B and HR-C are +6 and -7, respectively, favoring association of the two regions by electrostatic attraction.
source: In addition, the net charge of HR-A/B and HR-C are +6 and -7, respectively, favoring association of the two regions by electrostatic attraction.
evidence: This is based on calculation of net charges from the amino acid sequence.

claim: At high concentrations of HSF1 association of HR-A/B regions of several HSF1 molecules would be able to compete with the intramolecular reaction, forming the thermodynamically more stable trimer.
source: Only at high concentrations of HSF1 association of HR-A/B regions of several HSF1 molecules, which are in the open conformation, would be able to compete with the intramolecular reaction, forming the thermodynamically more stable trimer.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model to explain concentration-dependent trimerization.

claim: Temperature-induced unfolding of HR-C in the closed conformation favors HR-C dissociation.
source: Temperature-induced unfolding of HR-C in the closed conformation favors HR-C dissociation.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism based on the HX-MS data.

claim: HR-C unfolding in the open conformation prevents coiled-coil interaction with HR-A/B and thus reduces the back-reaction to the closed conformation.
source: Alternatively or in addition, HR-C unfolding in the open conformation prevents coiled-coil interaction with HR-A/B and thus reduces the back-reaction to the closed conformation.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism.

claim: Single helices free in solutions are usually not stable but are in a rapid equilibrium with the unfolded state.
source: For two reasons we do not consider this model as very likely: First, single helices free in solutions are usually not stable but are in a rapid equilibrium with the unfolded state due to the low energy difference between helix-internal hydrogen bonds and hydrogen bonds with water.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of protein structure.

claim: The average energy to unfold a protein which does not contain a co-factor is 1.4 kJ·mol-1.
source: Furthermore, the average energy to unfold a protein which does not contain a co-factor is 1.4 kJ·mol-1 (Privalov and Gill, 1988; Alexander et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dividing the activation energy for HR-C unfolding (249 kJ·mol-1) by 1.4 results in 175, suggesting that 175 residues are involved in the unfolding process.
source: Dividing the activation energy for HR-C unfolding determined by us, 249 kJ·mol-1, by 1.4 results in 175, suggesting that 175 residues are involved in this unfolding process.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the measured activation energy and literature values.

claim: 175 residues is close to 168, the number of residues corresponding to a dimer of the coiled-coil between HR-C (42 residues) with a similar sized region in HR-A/B.
source: This is close to 168, the number of residues corresponding to a dimer of the coiled-coil between HR-C (42 residues) with a similar sized region in HR-A/B.
evidence: This is a calculation supporting the dimer activation model.

claim: The dimer activation model assumes that the proposed Hsf1 dimer has a lower Tm than the Hsf1 monomer.
source: Our dimer activation model assumes that the proposed Hsf1 dimer has a lower Tm (Tm,D) than the Hsf1 monomer and that the measured Tm depends on the fraction of Hsf1 dimer present in the assay.
evidence: This is an assumption of the proposed model.

claim: Using relative quantification data for 11 different cancer cell lines results in Hsf1 concentrations between 10 and 130 nM.
source: Although there are no concentration determinations for Hsf1 in different tissues available to our knowledge, using the relative quantification data determined by mass spectrometry for 11 different cancer cell lines (Geiger et al., 2012), and assuming that these cells have a total protein concentration of about 150 mg/ml as determined for HEK293 cells (Gillen and Forbush, 1999), results in Hsf1 concentrations between 10 and 130 nM.
evidence: This is a calculation based on literature data with citations.

claim: Various stress conditions prevent Hsf1 export out of the nucleus, resulting in a locally increased Hsf1 concentration between 4- and 17-fold.
source: However, Hsf1 is not equally distributed throughout the cytosol but shuttles in and out of the nucleus with various stress conditions preventing Hsf1 export out of the nucleus (Vujanac et al., 2005), resulting in a locally increased Hsf1 concentration between 4- and 17-fold (Fujioka et al., 2006) and a local concentration between 40 and 2210 nM.
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: The recent crystal structure of the trimerization domain of the Hsf1 homolog Skn7 of Chaetomium thermophilum contains trimers but also tetramers.
source: Interestingly, the recent crystal structure of the trimerization domain of the Hsf1 homolog Skn7 of Chaetomium thermophilum contains trimers but also tetramers (PDB ID 5D5Z and 5D5Y, [Neudegger et al., 2016]).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a structural study.

claim: The tetramer structure of Skn7 might be a proxy for the dimer of HR-C-HR-A/B coiled-coils.
source: This tetramer might be a proxy for the dimer of HR-C-HR-A/B coiled-coils.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural similarity.

claim: Hsp90 could modulate the monomer-trimer transition by stabilizing HR-A-HR-A interactions and/or destabilize HR-A/B-HR-C interactions.
source: Hsp90 could modulate the monomer-trimer transition by stabilizing HR-A-HR-A interactions and/or destabilize HR-A/B-HR-C interactions, resulting in a reduced dimer dissociation rate and an increased rate of trimerization at lower temperatures.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism to explain the effects of Hsp90.

claim: Chaperones have been shown to locally unfold native proteins.
source: Chaperones have been shown to locally unfold native proteins (Rodriguez et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2010; Kirschke et al., 2014) and Hsp90 is believed to destabilize an α-helix in steroid hormone receptors to allow hormone binding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Hsp90 is believed to destabilize an α-helix in steroid hormone receptors to allow hormone binding.
source: Chaperones have been shown to locally unfold native proteins (Rodriguez et al., 2008; Sharma et al., 2010; Kirschke et al., 2014) and Hsp90 is believed to destabilize an α-helix in steroid hormone receptors to allow hormone binding.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Hsp90 function.

claim: Hsf1 exists in a monomer-dimer equilibrium.
source: According to our model Hsf1 exists in a monomer-dimer equilibrium, and trimerization of Hsf1 with subsequent DNA binding may occur continuously at low levels, promoted by Hsp90, as shown by us, and inhibited by TriC/CCT (Neef et al., 2014).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Trimerization of Hsf1 with subsequent DNA binding may occur continuously at low levels under non-stress conditions.
source: According to our model Hsf1 exists in a monomer-dimer equilibrium, and trimerization of Hsf1 with subsequent DNA binding may occur continuously at low levels, promoted by Hsp90, as shown by us, and inhibited by TriC/CCT (Neef et al., 2014).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: Basal Hsf1 transcriptional activity under non-stress conditions is ensured by low-level trimerization.
source: This may ensure basal Hsf1 transcriptional activity under non-stress conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the model.

claim: Any condition that would favor Hsf1 dimerization and thus trimerization or inhibit chaperone-mediated inhibition or attenuation would increase heat shock gene transcription.
source: Any condition that would favor Hsf1 dimerization and thus trimerization or inhibit chaperone-mediated inhibition or attenuation would, as a consequence, increase heat shock gene transcription.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claim: All of the conditions that activate Hsf1 have been associated with an imbalance in proteostasis affecting Hsf1 through titrating away chaperones.
source: All of the conditions mentioned above, including development, have been associated with an imbalance in proteostasis affecting Hsf1 through titrating away chaperones.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Hsf1 dimerization could be affected directly by changing its local concentration through transport into the nucleus or preventing its export.
source: However, Hsf1 dimerization could also be affected directly by changing its local concentration, as through transport of Hsf1 into the nucleus (Dai et al., 2003) or preventing its export (Vujanac et al., 2005), and by posttranslational modifications, including glutathionylation of the cysteine in HR-A in response to oxidative stress or alkylating agents (Liu et al., 1996), and phosphorylation of Thr142 in HR-A (Soncin et al., 2003), both of which would reduce the positive net charge of HR-A and thus the electrostatic repulsion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Glutathionylation of the cysteine in HR-A in response to oxidative stress or alkylating agents would reduce the positive net charge of HR-A and thus the electrostatic repulsion.
source: However, Hsf1 dimerization could also be affected directly by changing its local concentration, as through transport of Hsf1 into the nucleus (Dai et al., 2003) or preventing its export (Vujanac et al., 2005), and by posttranslational modifications, including glutathionylation of the cysteine in HR-A in response to oxidative stress or alkylating agents (Liu et al., 1996), and phosphorylation of Thr142 in HR-A (Soncin et al., 2003), both of which would reduce the positive net charge of HR-A and thus the electrostatic repulsion.
evidence: This is supported by citation and inference about charge effects.

claim: Phosphorylation of Thr142 in HR-A would reduce the positive net charge of HR-A and thus the electrostatic repulsion.
source: However, Hsf1 dimerization could also be affected directly by changing its local concentration, as through transport of Hsf1 into the nucleus (Dai et al., 2003) or preventing its export (Vujanac et al., 2005), and by posttranslational modifications, including glutathionylation of the cysteine in HR-A in response to oxidative stress or alkylating agents (Liu et al., 1996), and phosphorylation of Thr142 in HR-A (Soncin et al., 2003), both of which would reduce the positive net charge of HR-A and thus the electrostatic repulsion.
evidence: This is supported by citation and inference about charge effects.

claim: The model could explain why the temperature setpoint of activation was lower when human Hsf1 was expressed in Drosophila cells or in Xenopus oocytes.
source: Our model could explain why the temperature setpoint of activation was lower when human Hsf1 was expressed in Drosophila cells or in Xenopus oocytes (Baler et al., 1993; Clos et al., 1993).
evidence: This is a speculation about how the model explains previous observations, supported by citations.

claim: In transient or stable transfection experiments, the concentration of Hsf1 might have been much higher than is naturally the case in human cells.
source: In transient or stable transfection experiments, usually a strong promoter is used to express the transfected gene. Thus, the concentration of Hsf1 might have been much higher in the transfected cell than is naturally the case in human cells.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain previous observations.

claim: The kinetic Hsf1 activation model would allow each cell to adjust its setpoint of activation by changing the concentration of Hsf1.
source: Finally, our kinetic Hsf1 activation model would allow each cell to adjust its setpoint of activation by changing the concentration of Hsf1 by producing more Hsf1 or by concentrating it in a smaller compartment, for example by transport from the cytoplasm into the nucleus.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the proposed model.

claim: The model would explain the different setpoints in testis, mouse T-lymphocytes and mouse motor neurons.
source: This would easily explain the different setpoints in testis (Sarge et al., 1995; Sarge, 1995), mouse T-lymphocytes (Gothard et al., 2003) and mouse motor neurons (Batulan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a speculation about how the model explains tissue-specific differences, supported by citations.

claim: Hsf1 is a driver of malignancy in cancer cells.
source: This might be particularly important for cancer cells for which it was shown that Hsf1 is a driver of malignancy (Dai et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.
